unitTitle: Von Neumann Concept (Von-Neumann-Konzept) and Program Execution
overview: The concept describes a general-purpose computer controlled by a program that can solve different tasks and comprising four functional units (Die vier Werke). Programs and data reside as encoded contents in the same main memory (Hauptspeicher); the control unit (Leitwerk) generally executes instructions in sequence. Jumps (Sprünge) alter this flow. The unit also covers Harvard architecture (Harvard-Architektur), separate caches (getrennte Caches), linking (Linken), self-modifying code (Selbstmodifizierender Code), the stack (Stack) and stack frames (Stackframes), prologue and epilogue (Prolog und Epilog), and compiler optimization (Compileroptimierung).

entries.short: The stack is a memory region within byte-addressable main memory.
entries.explanation: The stack is not a separate memory device alongside main memory; it is managed within main memory. Like other memory contents, its contents reside at addressable byte locations.
entries.example: A program can use part of main memory for stack frames.
pitfalls: Do not treat the stack as a separate memory device alongside main memory.
entries.heading: Rückblick: Stackframes und Unterprogramme

entries.short: A stack frame is the region of stack memory associated with a routine call.
entries.explanation: When a routine is designed or compiled, its stack frame size and the locations of its variables within the frame are determined. Any required preservation of register values and release of the region on return must also be taken into account.
entries.example: A frame can contain space for local variables and saved registers.
pitfalls: Not all routines need stack frames of the same size.
entries.heading: Rückblick: Stackframes und Unterprogramme

entries.short: A routine’s prologue sets up its stack frame, and its epilogue tears it down on return.
entries.explanation: The prologue appears at the beginning of a routine and typically reserves the required stack space and saves any necessary values. The epilogue restores saved values, releases stack space, and prepares the return to the caller. The caller can then continue using the agreed result.
entries.example: A routine reserves stack space for local values in its prologue and releases it again in its epilogue.
pitfalls: Returning does not require all registers to remain unchanged.
entries.heading: Prolog und Epilog

entries.short: A calling convention specifies how routines handle arguments, results, and register values during calls and returns.
entries.explanation: It is the agreement that the caller and called routine must follow to work together. This includes which register values must be preserved; therefore, not all registers necessarily have to remain unchanged.
entries.example: If the calling convention requires a register to be preserved, the responsible routine saves and restores its value.
pitfalls: Not every register change after a call is an error; what matters is the agreement.
entries.heading: Prolog und Epilog

entries.short: Compiler optimization can change the instruction sequence, and -O2 denotes optimization level 2.
entries.explanation: A compiler can transform code so that, for example, register allocation or the instruction sequence differs from an unoptimized example. `-O2` denotes the stated optimization level 2. Optimization must preserve the effects required by the program that are observable from outside.
entries.example: A register that holds a value in an unoptimized example may be used differently in a program compiled with `-O2`.
pitfalls: Do not assume that a specific register allocation from an unoptimized example is mandatory.
entries.heading: Compileroptimierung

entries.short: The Von Neumann concept describes a general-purpose computer whose program controls the solution of different problems.
entries.explanation: The computer’s structure is independent of the particular problem to be solved. Instead of redesigning the hardware for each task, a different program controls the same general-purpose computer. The concept is described in an EDVAC paper.
entries.example: The same computer can calculate a sum or process characters using different programs.
pitfalls: Do not equate the concept with a single machine instruction or a particular application.
related: Programs and data in the same memory
entries.heading: Das Von-Neumann-Konzept

entries.short: The Von Neumann model divides the computer into main memory, a control unit, an arithmetic unit, and an input/output unit.
entries.explanation: Main memory, also called working memory, holds programs and data. The control unit executes the instruction cycle and controls the arithmetic unit; the arithmetic unit, usually called the ALU, performs arithmetic operations. The input/output unit handles input and output, including secondary storage.
entries.example: During a calculation, the control unit fetches instructions, controls the ALU, and uses data from main memory.
pitfalls: Arrows in a schematic model show general relationships, not every specific bus or data line.
entries.heading: Die vier Werke

entries.short: Main memory consists of equal-sized cells at consecutive addresses and, in the Von Neumann model, holds programs and data.
entries.explanation: Main memory is viewed as a sequence of equal-sized cells with consecutive addresses. It is byte-addressable, and the stack resides in this memory. In the Von Neumann model, it holds both program code and data.
entries.example: A sequence of memory cells with addresses 100, 101, and 102 illustrates consecutive addresses.
pitfalls: Do not confuse main memory with secondary storage, such as persistent data storage.
related: Programs and data in the same memory
entries.heading: Die Merkpunkte mit bereinigter Nummerierung

entries.term: programs and data in the same memory
entries.short: In the Von Neumann model, instructions and data reside together in main memory.
entries.explanation: Memory is not inherently divided into one main memory reserved only for programs and another reserved only for data. Instructions and data are different interpretations of encoded memory contents. Because programs reside in memory, the machine can in principle modify memory contents.
entries.example: Program code and a number processed by the program can both reside in the same main memory.
pitfalls: Shared memory does not automatically mean that every memory region is writable.
related: Encoded memory contents: data and instructions
entries.heading: Die Merkpunkte mit bereinigter Nummerierung

entries.term: encoded memory contents: data and instructions
entries.short: Data and instructions are stored as bit patterns whose meaning is determined by an agreed encoding.
entries.explanation: Numbers are represented in binary in a computer; data gets its meaning from the binary encoding and interpretation used. Instructions are encoded according to the ISA and can be displayed in a readable assembly representation. Memory therefore contains encoded values, not the printed words of the assembly representation.
entries.example: Depending on how it is interpreted, the same bit pattern can represent a number or an encoded instruction.
pitfalls: A bit pattern alone does not determine whether it is interpreted as a number, data value, or instruction.
related: Programs and data in the same memory
entries.heading: Daten und Befehle sind codierte Speicherinhalte

entries.short: MAR and MDR are names for registers associated with an address and data, respectively, during memory access.
entries.explanation: MDR stands for *Memory Data Register* and denotes a register for memory data. The lecture notes give “Memory Access Register” for MAR but mark that name for verification; *Memory Address Register* may have been intended. The precise sequence of a memory access is not specified.
entries.example: Under the usual naming convention, the MAR holds a memory address and the MDR holds the data transferred to or from that address.
pitfalls: The expanded name of MAR is not clearly established in the lecture notes.
entries.heading: Daten und Befehle sind codierte Speicherinhalte

entries.short: The instruction cycle is the sequence of operations carried out by the control unit to execute instructions.
entries.explanation: In the four-unit model, the control unit is responsible for carrying out the instruction cycle. The lecture notes do not specify its phases. The term places instruction processing within the computer’s control.
pitfalls: Do not infer a specific number or order of phases from the lecture notes.
entries.heading: Die vier Werke

entries.short: With sequential instruction execution, instructions are generally executed in their stored order.
entries.explanation: A program is a sequence of commands or instructions. They are generally stored at increasing addresses and executed one after another. Jumps can change their order.
entries.example: Without a jump, a program can execute the instruction at one address and then the following instruction.
pitfalls: Generally sequential does not mean that a program cannot contain jumps.
entries.heading: Die Merkpunkte mit bereinigter Nummerierung

entries.short: Conditional and unconditional jumps redirect instruction execution to another location.
entries.explanation: A jump changes the otherwise sequential order of instructions. A conditional jump redirects execution depending on a condition; an unconditional jump does so without checking a condition. This lets a program describe different flows of execution.
entries.example: A conditional jump can branch to a later instruction when its condition is met.
pitfalls: Jumps change the control flow; they do not automatically change the program code.
entries.heading: Die Merkpunkte mit bereinigter Nummerierung

entries.short: The Harvard architecture uses separate memories for program code and data.
entries.explanation: Its memory organization differs from the Von Neumann model, in which programs and data reside in the same main memory. Separating the memories is an architectural choice and, by itself, says nothing about whether individual memory regions are write-protected.
entries.example: A system with a dedicated program memory and a dedicated data memory follows the described Harvard organization.
pitfalls: Do not equate Harvard architecture with write protection.
related: Programs and data in the same memory
entries.heading: Gemeinsamer oder getrennter Speicher?

entries.term: shared main memory with separate caches
entries.short: A hybrid organization uses shared main memory but separate caches for instructions and data.
entries.explanation: With this memory organization, programs and data reside in the same main memory. Instructions and data can nevertheless be held in separate caches for faster access. Main memory organization and cache organization describe different levels.
entries.example: A processor can have separate instruction and data caches even though both access the same main memory.
pitfalls: Separate caches do not automatically mean separate main memories.
related: Programs and data in the same memory
entries.heading: Gemeinsamer oder getrennter Speicher?

entries.short: Write protection and separating program memory from data memory are independent properties.
entries.explanation: A memory region can be treated as modifiable or non-modifiable. This is a separate question from whether programs and data reside in shared or separate memories. A shared main memory can therefore contain regions with different levels of modifiability.
entries.example: A shared memory can contain a write-protected region for code and a writable region for data.
pitfalls: Do not infer from shared memory that every content may be overwritten.
related: Programs and data in the same memory
Shared main memory with separate caches
entries.heading: Gemeinsamer oder getrennter Speicher?

entries.short: When programs reside in memory, the machine can in principle modify their memory contents.
entries.explanation: The Von Neumann model places programs and data in the same main memory, so program code is present as memory contents. Modifying programs in memory is relevant, among other contexts, to operating systems and to adjustments made to programs during linking. This does not mean that a program constantly modifies its own code during normal execution.
entries.example: After combining program parts, a linker can adjust certain address references in the program.
pitfalls: The ability to modify program code is not the same as self-modifying code.
related: Programs and data in the same memory
entries.heading: Programme im Speicher verändern

entries.short: During linking, a linker combines compiled program parts and libraries into a program and resolves references.
entries.explanation:
The linker combines related compiled program parts and required library components into a program. It resolves references between the parts and, where necessary, adjusts address information. This process follows compilation of the program parts.

1. Gather the compiled program parts and required library components.
2. Resolve references between the parts.
3. Adjust address information if necessary.
entries.example: If a program contains a call to `printf`, the reference must be resolved during linking to a suitable target in a library.
pitfalls: Do not confuse linking with compiling the source code.
entries.heading: Was bedeutet Linken?

entries.short: Self-modifying code changes its own program code during execution.
entries.explanation: A program writes to memory regions where its own code resides. This technique is now a rare exception. Different execution flows are usually implemented with conditional jumps and changes to addresses.
entries.example: A program that overwrites one of its own instructions at runtime would be self-modifying.
pitfalls: A linker that adjusts address information while combining program parts is not automatically self-modifying code.
entries.heading: Selbstmodifizierender Code
